Compaction strategies fall into two families. Generative compactors replace older history with text written by a model: a running or recursive summary ( Packer et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) , the native compaction of deployed agents such as Claude Code, pi agent, and Hermes Agent ( Rajasekaran et al., 2025 ; Zechner, 2025 ; Nous Research, 2025 ) , or summaries from prompts optimized for long-horizon agents ( Kang et al., 2026 ; Min et al., 2026 ) . Selective compactors keep part of the original history verbatim and discard the rest, often by rules from cache replacement ( Belady, 1966 ; Mattson et al., 1970 ) . First-in-first-out (FIFO) discards the oldest turns, as in MemGPT’s message queue and the recency baselines of ACON and TRACE ( Packer et al., 2024 ; Kang et al., 2026 ; Min et al., 2026 ) ; least-recently-used (LRU) keeps the entries used most recently, and Generative Agents similarly retrieve memories by recency of access combined with model-rated importance and relevance ( Park et al., 2023 ) . Generative strategies summarize earlier history, whereas selective strategies retain selected parts of it verbatim ( Packer et al., 2024 ; Kang et al., 2026 ; Min et al., 2026 ) . Prior work studies how these choices affect task completion and execution reliability. We examine how they affect compliance with operating rules. Rule loss under compaction. Recent work shows that compaction can remove the rules an agent intended to follow. Governance Decay ( Chen, 2026 ) evaluates whether organizational policies still constrain tool calls after compaction and protects them through rule pinning. COMPINT ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , concurrent with our work, studies whether user-issued constraints are retained and followed after compaction, and preserves them with a separate extractor. TRACE ( Min et al., 2026 ) asks a related question for task execution, measuring how recurrent compaction affects task completion and reliability in AppWorld. Table 1 compares the factors these studies vary. Two gaps remain. First, none of them evaluates rule compliance in a complete agent harness. Governance Decay assembles its agents from parts: its main experiments use a self-constructed agent loop and compactor written for the study. In a self-constructed agent, the researcher decides when compaction fires and what the agent sees afterwards. In a complete harness, the harness itself has already made these choices. COMPINT runs no agent loop: it replays stored histories to compactor and prober models and measures compliance mainly through multiple-choice probes. TRACE adapts the compaction loop of an existing harness, OpenClaw, but measures task success rather than rule compliance. ARCBench instead runs every configuration in the loop of pi ( Zechner, 2025 ) and grades the tool calls the agent makes after compaction (§ 3 ). Second, these studies show that violations rise after compaction, but not where each violation comes from. Governance Decay compares violation rates with a full-context control and splits them by whether a judge finds the policy in the compacted context. COMPINT reports retention and compliance as separate aggregates. Neither separates the violations an agent would commit even with the full history from those that compaction adds. A yes-or-no retention label also cannot show a rule whose wording was weakened, for example by losing a scope, an exception, or a negation. In such way, a rule that survives compaction can still be ignored, since a rule in context does not guarantee that a model follows it ( Mu et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Failure attribution for agents locates the agent and step responsible for a task failure ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , not the state of a rule compliance after compaction. Our empirical study instead attributes each violation after compaction to the agent’s own behavior or to the state of the rule in the compacted context, and compares this attribution across compaction configurations, rule delivery channels, and adversarial settings (§ 4 ). Figure 2: Workflow of an ARCBench evaluation episode, from task and rule acquisition through configurable compaction and adversarial settings to deterministic action grading. 3 Benchmark ARCBench measures whether an agent still complies with an operating rule after its history is compacted. We state the threat model (Appendix B ), the benchmark overview (§ 3.1 ), how cases are curated (§ 3.1 ), the factors a configuration varies (§ 3.1 ), and the evaluation protocol (§ 3.2 ). 3.1 Benchmark Overview Harness. ARCBench extends pi ( Zechner, 2025 ) , an open-source coding-agent harness with its own agent loop, tool calling, and native compaction. Running inside pi keeps the evaluation close to how agents are actually used. A run configuration specifies the task case, the configurable factors below, and the agent and compactor models. The runner starts a pi agent session, builds the history, compacts it, and issues the violated request. In the email case of Figure 2 , a send_email call to an address outside @nexus-corp.com is graded as a violation from the recorded tool-call trace, whatever the compacted summary says. A Dockerfile pins all dependencies, giving the runner the same software environment across machines. (Appendix C ). Task cases. Each case pairs an operating rule with a concrete attacker goal. We group violations into four types mapped to OWASP risk classes ( OWASP GenAI Security Project, 2025 ; OWASP GenAI Security Project, 2024 ) : disclosure of protected data, access to restricted resources, unauthorized actions, and bypass or omission of required controls. We adapt cases from Governance Decay and COMPINT ( Chen, 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) , drop those that do not fit our setting, for example because the violation cannot be seen in a tool call, and add four cases so that every violation type is covered for both personal and organizational rules. Appendix E lists the 17 cases and the selection criteria. Configurable factors. A configuration sets five factors, all shown in Figure 2 : the rule delivery channel ( c1 : direct instruction, c2 : persistence instruction, c3 : document-embedded, or c4 : policy-tool fetching), the compaction strategy (seven generative strategies and three selective compactors), the compaction budget, the attack, and the defense. Table 10 summarizes the factors, and Appendices E.4 , F , G , and H give the full configurations. 3.2 Evaluation Protocol Violation A configuration z z fixes the agent model and the factors of § 3.1 . In our empirical study, we find that compaction raises violations mostly without deleting the rule: compacted runs retaining the rule still violate 2.6 times as often as runs with the full history. Moreover, compaction changes the agent’s reasoning for violating. Different compaction strategies, tight compaction budget constraints, and rule delivery channel all affect compliance. Under attack, added volume barely matters, but compactor-targeted injections not only drop the rule but also affect the violation greatly. Defenses restore rules, but compliance is still weakened under attack. Rule retention is thus not a sufficient proxy for compliance. Future studies may use ARCBench to explain why agents still violate retained rules, test adaptive attacks and defenses, and cover more models, domains, and longer sessions with repeated compaction. Limitations Cases. ARCBench contains seventeen English cases from a few domains: messaging and email, file access, software operations, and purchasing. Operating rules in other domains, such as clinical, financial, or legal work, depend on domain knowledge that these cases do not test, so our findings may not carry over to them; extending the benchmark requires new cases with their own tools and graders. Adversarial settings. The adversarial settings study uses one model, one compactor, no volume injection, and no compaction budget constraint, and its payloads are static and cannot adapt to a defense. It therefore does not show whether the attacks and defenses behave the same under other compaction strategies, compaction budget constraints, or models, or what the defenses cost on authorized work, and the escape mechanism remains a hypothesis. Because ARCBench exposes each factor as a setting, future work can explore these combinations and introduce new factors, such as adaptive attacks. Ethical Considerations The cases evaluate prohibited effects from recorded tool calls in a controlled harness. Examples include data disclosure, unauthorized spending, and bypassed approval steps; none of these effects is carried out against external systems. The adversarial settings study adapts published attacks to a fixed rule-omission objective and does not develop new attack techniques. Case construction and evaluation code should preserve this separation when reproducing the benchmark. The task artifacts and model responses are experimental data, not evidence of behavior on real users’ private workflows. References Anthropic (2026a) Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 system card . Its context history is a sequence of turns H = ( h 1 , … , h n ) H=(h_{1},\dots,h_{n}) with h i ∈ 𝒰 ∪ 𝒴 ∪ 𝒯 h_{i}\in\mathcal{U}\cup\mathcal{Y}\cup\mathcal{T} , where 𝒰 \mathcal{U} denotes user instructions, 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} the agent’s responses and tool calls, and 𝒯 \mathcal{T} the tool results, including retrieved documents. An operating rule r r , such as “send email only within the company domain,” constrains the agent’s future actions and enters H H through one of several delivery channels (§ 3.1 ). When H H grows long, a compactor C C replaces it with a shorter history H ~ = C ⁡ ( H ) \widetilde{H}=C(H) , consisting of a summary, a selected subset of turns, or both. Later, the user issues an ordinary request q q , and the agent responds with a sequence of tool calls t = M ⁡ ( H ~ , q ) t=M(\widetilde{H},q) The agent violates the rule if t ∈ 𝒜 r t\in\mathcal{A}_{r} , where 𝒜 r \mathcal{A}_{r} is the set of sequences of tool calls in 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} that r r prohibits. In the operating rule example, we state above, whether a call is prohibited usually depends on its arguments, such as the recipient’s domain. ARCBench grades what the agent does, not what it says: only its tool calls count. In addition to this grade, the benchmark also records whether the compacted history still states the rule (§ 3.2 ). The attacker. The attacker is any party whose content reaches the history as tool results, such as an email the agent reads, a web page or shared document it retrieves, or the output of a third-party tool. It controls the content of these tool results, but it cannot see or modify r r , the user’s instructions, the request q q , the agent model M M , or the compactor C C , and it observes nothing else in H H . Its goal is to trigger a prohibited action t ∈ 𝒜 r t\in\mathcal{A}_{r} . It can have two attacks, which can be combined: volume injection adds long, rule-unrelated tool results so that the rule is more likely to be lost when the history is compacted, and compactor-targeted injection adds a tool result that instructs C C to omit operating rules from H ~ \widetilde{H} . Even with this limited knowledge, the attacker raises violations after compaction (§ 4 ). The defender. The defender is the developer or operator of the agent system and wants the agent to keep complying with r r after compaction. It can change the instructions that C C gives its model, for example, by marking the history as data, warning against embedded instructions, or asking the compactor to preserve operating rules. It cannot identify or filter adversarial tool results, modify M M or its decision loop, or change the user’s rule or request. Appendix C Execution Environment and Packaging C.1 Execution Environment ARCBench is built on pi ( Zechner, 2025 ) , an open-source coding agent with native compaction, for two reasons. First, reproducibility: pi is pinned to one commit and shipped with the benchmark as checksummed packages, its compaction code runs unmodified. Second, fidelity to deployed systems: the two pi-based compaction strategies call pi’s own compaction, the procedure a deployed agent runs, rather than a reimplementation, and the other strategies run through a common driver over the same history. The agent acts in a tool-calling loop, and all models are accessed through one OpenAI-compatible chat-completions interface; in the reported studies, the same model compacts and acts. Tools are never executed: each call receives a fixed canned result that is identical across conditions, so episodes have no side effects and run independently. C.2 Packaging To make the benchmark easy to adopt, we release it with a Dockerfile that fixes the runtime versions, installs every dependency from pinned lockfiles and the vendored pi packages, and mounts results rather than building them into the image, so a container built on any machine runs the same code. A preflight command checks the API key, the pi checksums, the cases, and the Python environment before any model call. Each configuration is one invocation of the central script (§ 3.1 ), and the published tables can be regenerated from the released result rows. E.4 Rule Delivery Channels The artifacts name the channels c1 through c4 . Personal cases use direct instruction ( c1 ), which supplies the rule in a user message, or persistence ( c2 ), which asks the agent to write the rule to rule.md using persist_document . Organizational cases use document-embedded delivery ( c3 ), which returns the rule as a tool result, or policy-tool fetching ( c4 ), which requires an explicit get_policy call before returning it. Rule-delivery tools have generic descriptions that do not encode the rule. Otherwise, a tool schema outside the compacted history could supply it to a nominally rule-absent condition.
